{{Short description|None}}
{{Use American English|date=September 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=July 2023}}

The [[governor of Texas]] is the [[chief executive officer]] of the [[U.S. state]] of [[Texas]] and the commander in chief of the state’s military forces. The incumbent governor is Greg Abbott, who assumed office on January 20, 2015. Since [[Admission to the Union|Texas' statehood]] in 1845, 45 individuals have served in 48 governorships. The discrepancy is due to the nonconsecutive terms of [[Elisha M. Pease]], [[Miriam A. Ferguson]], and [[Bill Clements]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Association |first=Texas State Historical |title=History and Powers of the Governor of Texas |url=https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/governor |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=Texas State Historical Association |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Governors |url=https://txfgm.org/the-governors/ |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=Friends of the Governor's Mansion |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Governors of Texas - Texas Legislative Reference Library |url=https://lrl.texas.gov/legeleaders/governors/govBrowse.cfm |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=lrl.texas.gov}}</ref>

When compared to those of other states, the governorship of Texas has been described as one of relative weakness.<ref name="slate">{{Cite web |last=Suellentrop, Chip |date=2000-01-05 |title=Is George W. Bush a "Weak" Governor? |url=http://www.slate.com/id/1004307/ |access-date=2010-01-25 |publisher=Slate Magazine - Explainer}}</ref><ref name="molly">{{Cite book |last=Ivins, Molly |title=Shrub: The Short But Happy Political Life of George W. Bush |last2=Lou Dubose |publisher=Vintage Books |year=2000 |isbn=0-375-75714-7 |location=New York |pages=xii-xiii |author-link=Molly Ivins}}</ref> In some respects, it is the [[Lieutenant Governor of Texas|lieutenant governor of Texas]], who presides over the [[Texas Senate]], who possesses greater influence to exercise their prerogatives.<ref name=slate/><ref name=molly/>

== Governors ==
{{for|the period before annexation|List of Texas governors and presidents}}

Texas was [[Texas annexation|annexed]] by the [[United States]] and [[admission to the Union|admitted to the Union]] on December 29, 1845.<ref>{{usstat|9|108}}</ref>

The governor is inaugurated on the third Tuesday of January every four years along with the lieutenant governor, and serves a term of four years. Prior to the present laws, in 1845, the state's first constitution established the office of governor, serving a term of two years, but no more than four years of every six.<ref>1845 Const. Art V sec 4</ref> The 1861 constitution, following [[Secession in the United States|secession]] from the Union, established the first Monday of November following election as the term's start.<ref>1861 Const. art V sec 12</ref> Following the end of the [[American Civil War]], the 1866 constitution increased term length to four years, limiting overall service to no more than eight years of every twelve, moving the term's start to the first Thursday following organization of the legislature, or "as soon thereafter as practicable."<ref>1866 Const. art V sec 4</ref> The constitution of 1869, enacted during [[Reconstruction era of the United States|Reconstruction]], removed term limitations,<ref>1869 Const. Art IV sec 4</ref> to this day making Texas one of sixteen states, territory or jurisdiction (including the U.S. Territory [[Puerto Rico]] and the [[District of Columbia]]<ref>[http://www.nga.org/files/pdf/BOS4-9.pdf Executive Branch] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629023725/http://www.nga.org/files/pdf/BOS4-9.pdf|date=2011-06-29 }} retrieved 23-October-2008</ref> with no [[Term limits in the United States#Gubernatorial term limits|limit]] on gubernatorial terms. The present constitution of 1876 returned terms to two years,<ref>TX Const. Art IV sec 4</ref> but a 1972 amendment again returned them to four.<ref>[http://texaspolitics.laits.utexas.edu/1_3_1.html Texas Politics - The Executive Branch] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090211001255/http://texaspolitics.laits.utexas.edu/1_3_1.html|date=2009-02-11 }}. Texaspolitics.laits.utexas.edu. Retrieved on 2013-07-15.</ref>

In the case of a vacancy in the office, the lieutenant governor becomes governor.<ref>TX Const. art IV sec 16 graf d</ref> Prior to a 1999 amendment, the lieutenant governor only acted as governor until the expiration of the term to which he succeeded.<ref>Under the 1861 constitution, law provided that the lieutenant governor would be "styled Governor of those state of Republicans" in case of vacancy.</ref><ref>1861 Const art V sec 12</ref> The governor and the lieutenant governor are not officially elected on the same ticket.
